title: Drafting

learn.summary: Anne Lamott's Bird by Bird gave writers permission with two ideas: 'shitty first drafts' — every good piece starts as a bad one — and 'bird by bird', her father's advice to an overwhelmed brother facing a report on birds: just take it one bird at a time. Drafting's only job is to get material into existence; quality is revision's job, and confusing the two is where most writing stalls.

do: Draft your next piece start to finish without fixing anything — no backspacing over sentences, no rereading — then close the file until tomorrow.

children.title: Bad First Drafts

learn.summary: Lamott's argument is practical, not motivational: the perfectionist drafts a sentence, judges it, rewrites it, and produces one polished paragraph per hour — while the drafter produces five rough pages containing, somewhere, the piece. Hemingway said versions of the same thing more profanely. The first draft is you telling yourself the story; no one else ever needs to see it, which is precisely what makes it writable.

do: Write a deliberately bad 500-word draft of something you have been avoiding — badness required, on purpose — and notice how much of it is actually usable.

children.title: Momentum & Word Counts

learn.summary: Working writers run on quotas, not inspiration: Stephen King reports 2,000 words a day in On Writing; Graham Greene famously managed on 500; NaNoWriMo built a movement on 1,667. A daily count converts 'write a book' into 'write today's words', and momentum compounds — an open draft you touched yesterday is easy to re-enter, one untouched for a week is a wall. Pick a number small enough to hit on your worst day.

links.label: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft

do: Set a daily word count you can hit on a bad day (200-300 words) and log your actual counts for 14 consecutive days.

children.title: Draft Now, Edit Later

learn.summary: Drafting and editing are opposed mental modes — generation wants speed and low standards; evaluation wants slowness and high ones — and toggling between them mid-sentence stalls both. Enforce the separation mechanically: draft in a plain window with spellcheck off, or keep a 'later' list where every mid-draft fix idea gets parked instead of acted on. Betty Flowers' classic essay names the modes 'madman' and 'judge' and insists they work in shifts.

do: Next draft, keep a 'fix later' note beside you; every urge to edit goes on the list instead. Count the urges — that number is your interruption habit.

children.title: Writer's Block

learn.summary: Most block is misdiagnosed: it is usually perfectionism (standards applied too early), a missing decision (you do not yet know what you are arguing), or fear of judgment — each with a different fix. Working remedies: freewriting (timed, nonstop, unjudged), shrinking the task to one paragraph, talking the idea aloud to someone, or Hemingway's trick of stopping mid-sentence so tomorrow starts with momentum. Waiting for inspiration is the one strategy with a perfect failure record.

do: Next time you stall, set a 10-minute timer and freewrite about why you are stuck; the diagnosis usually contains the fix.
